activity.title: Buildbox (YC S26) finds user-facing agent failures hidden behind successful traces and evals. The most expensive agent failures rarely look like errors. An agent can pass its evals and look healthy in traces while still failing to help users complete important tasks. They ask again, redirect the agent, try a workaround, or give up. Teams usually uncover these patterns after they’ve already affected customers. Buildbox is agent analytics built around user outcomes. We find where important journeys break down, show how often it happens and who it affects, and connect those failures to activation, conversion, and retention. Buildbox then tests better agent behaviors and product experiences, giving teams evidence-backed fixes to review and ship. Founders Mark Nour and Trishala Jain met at UC Berkeley and have been building together for the past three years. Across teams at Netflix, Google, Amazon, and MongoDB, they saw the same pattern: companies had plenty of signals & observability, but finding the issues that actually mattered and turning them into a fix still took a lot of manual detective work. Congrats on the launch, Mark and Trishala! 🚀 https://lnkd.in/g-BEkwhg ...more ...more

Mireye (YC S26) builds the infrastructure that lets AI agents reason and act in the physical world. Every AI agent today lives entirely on the internet. Most of the economy happens in the physical world, and models are blind to it. Ask about a real place, and you get a guess, and in the real world, guesses cost real money when stakes are high. No single tool or platform has this data. It's spread across thousands of them, each one built for humans, none for agents. Mireye is one API and MCP that connects agents to the physical world: data, enrichment, tools, and signals that power them to make decisions. Every answer cited. Their first customers built agents that source off-market land deals 100x faster than before, and work that took analysts weeks now takes agents minutes. Founder Ansh Chokshi sold his first startup, Poker Pit, at the age of 21 after growing it from zero to $250K ARR in four months. He then led AI/ML engineering at Seismic. Today Mireye launches the first on-demand indexing API for the physical world. Ask for data that isn't indexed, and its long-running agent sources it and indexes it on the fly. If you're working on anything where AI meets the physical world (robotics, logistics, real estate, insurance, energy), Ansh would love to chat: ansh@mireye.com Congrats on the launch, Ansh! 🚀 https://lnkd.in/gx2VXYTs ...more ...more

Introducing Clayzo , the best way to make everyone on the team a product builder. 🎉 Product and design are converging into a single full-stack builder role. PMs and designers are using Claude Code and Cursor to ship changes directly to production. But these tools give people total freedom with no guardrails. It’s pure vibe coding, no awareness of your codebase. Engineers end up reviewing broken PRs and cleaning up work that was never ready for production. That's not what "making everyone a builder" should look like. With Clayzo , anyone can safely iterate on their existing product in an interface they are used to (not the IDE!), with built-in guardrails to prevent them from accidentally touching sensitive parts of the code. We abstract away all developer context, making it super easy to spin up your product in just two clicks and start working on it right away. Used by some of the fastest growing companies in the world and we're opening it up to more teams now. DM if you want in! ...more

"Don't let the B+ be the enemy of the A." The biggest difference between a B+ and an A idea is really just grit. As Mark Pincus (co-founder of Zynga ) put it at Founders, Inc. today, you need to be willing to put 10 years of your life creating multiple B+ companies with no real guarantee that it will turn into an A. Everyone's founder journey looks different, but there were a few things from the talk that really stuck with me: → Trust your gut, especially when building in consumer. Ask yourself if you would actually use the product on a consistent basis. → Bet on consumer behavior staying the same instead of changing. It's really hard to get people to change their habits, so if you can build alongside a pattern that already works, go with that. → Don't say "they don't get the vision yet" when building in consumer. People need to get it right away, otherwise it's probably not the right product. Thank you Hubert Thieblot and Founders, Inc. for hosting! 👏 ...more

Turns out the best workflow for designers using AI isn't "tell the agent to do everything." It's a mix of doing the small tweaks yourself and letting the agent handle the bigger lifts. I spoke to an experienced designer today and one of her favorite parts about our product was that she can make simple tweaks like font, color, or copy directly on the design side, and then just tell the agent to execute the bigger changes. A few reasons why this workflow is better: → Way more efficient. Small tweaks don't need a full agent loop, you just do them yourself in seconds. → The agent messes up less. Pointing to precise elements gives it way better context, so the output is much more accurate. → Bonus: less token usage on the simple stuff It was really cool to hear how designers are thinking about using AI in their day-to-day. Excited to keep building with this kind of feedback in mind! 🚀 ...more

I never knew what freedom felt like until my first paycheck. Money has always been a taboo topic that people steer away from and it's easy to avoid bringing it up in general. So when I got my first paycheck from Siemens at 19, I didn't know how to process it. I remember staring at my bank account and seeing the biggest deposit at that point I'd ever seen before. I couldn't believe that I finally managed to earn money through my own work, and it wasn't disbursed to me from the school or given to me by my parents. It was 𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗲. It felt like validation that I belonged in a job market that I never thought I'd belong to. And it was a realization that I was finally capable of making my own income at such a young age. ► Because I was making more as a 𝗽𝗮𝗿𝘁-𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗻 than what a 𝘀𝗲𝗻𝗶𝗼𝗿 𝗦𝗪𝗘 would make in Taiwan 𝘪𝘯 𝘢 𝘮𝘰𝘯𝘵𝘩. ► Because my dad would tell me how he worked at KFC when he was 19 and how he's 𝙨𝙤 𝙥𝙧𝙤𝙪𝙙 that his daughters at 19 are working big tech jobs that he could've never imagined for himself at the same age. ► Because I was laid off once and I had doubted where I stood in this job market until the paycheck gave me evidence that I deserved a place. It's freedom. It's independence. It's the kind of autonomy you don't get from moving to college or starting a new opportunity. Making your own money at a young age gives you options you didn't know existed. Now that I'm on my third internship with ServiceNow, my intern salaries throughout my university years had allowed me to pay for my own flights to travel to places like Portugal, Slovakia, Japan, Korea, Taiwan, and more. I visited friends in Boston, Seattle, Hawaii, and even went to Chicago for the first time last weekend. I paid for LinkedIn Premium to grow my presence here and for hosting CareerNow, which led me to winning the $25k Taco Bell scholarship. 𝗡𝗼𝗻𝗲 of that would have happened 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘁 my own money to spend. Everyone talks about full-time salaries. But what about the first intern paycheck for a 19-year-old who's never worked a real job before? That's a conversation we don't have enough. It's a domino effect. By creating an environment of independence for yourself, it truly opens more doors for you than you could ever imagine. What doors did your first intern paycheck open for you? 👇 _____________ 💙 Like or share so more students see this ☻ Follow Arlina Yang for more on the early career journey 📷 My twin Andrea and I at Boston 🍁

I left my job, moved across the country to San Francisco, and started building Suzanne Here’s the TL;DR of what I’ve learned: 𝟭. 𝗬𝗼𝘂 𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗼𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝘀𝘆𝗻𝗱𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗲. The stories you see on X and LinkedIn are outliers: raised $8M in 2 months, went viral overnight, hit $2M ARR from a Lovable MVP. Building something from 0 is hard, and you don’t see the thousands of people building for years before things take off. Don’t let someone else’s highlight reel make you feel behind. 𝟮. 𝗝𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗮𝘀𝗸. Want an introduction? Want to meet someone? Want to try something you don’t feel qualified for? Ask. People are much more willing to help than you’d expect. 𝟯. 𝗕𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗴𝗹𝗮𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗼𝘂𝘀. Social media makes building look like vibecoding an app in a week, landing huge contracts, and going viral. The reality is a lot of rejection, and questioning yourself every day. The highs are incredibly rewarding, but they come with some pretty low lows. 𝟰. 𝗦𝗽𝗲𝗲𝗱 >>>> I’ve learned more from shipping and talking to users than I ever did from planning to start a company. The best way to learn is by "actually doing the thing". 𝟱. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗺𝗲𝗲𝘁 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿. Make time for people, coffee can turn into a friendship, a cold DM can turn into a customer, and a random introduction can completely change your trajectory. Building a company is a people game first. Moving to SF has introduced me to some of the smartest and most ambitious I’ve ever met (shout out Ethan Wang & Mann Bellani ) Still learning + building more & more every day.

I've been getting the WORST COMPLIMENT lately and it's been pissing me off Context: I genuinely love writing, which is kinda what has fueled so much of my Linkedin writing journey and posts. Started cause like typical asian child I had to prep for my SAT/ACTs back in the day for hours after school - and a huge part of that was writing essays. So, I've taken ways to incorporate that in my adult life. I journal regularly and for 'work' I do a lot of content creation - marketing copies, sales copies, etc. Now, the problem? "Wait is this written by AI?" NO BRO I LITERALLY WROTE THIS LETTER BY LETTER CLACKING AWAY ON MY KEYBOARD 😭😭😭😭 The first time it happened I was so taken aback, "how could you think AI wrote this? there's so much personality to it??" This was when I actually was helping another founder with his personal brand and wrote a few pieces for him. And then it kept happening with multiple people. I was helping other friends with outreach messages, content, deck material. At a certain point I thought it was funny actually. But recently it's been concerning. Linkedin obvio released a new "seems like AI slop" button - but that's not even the point. All of the context LLMs have been fed with are ORIGINAL HUMAN WRITTEN PIECES. So of course it will sounds like a super polished person writing. There's obviously tell tale signs of ai writing; 1️⃣ "—" The em dash, originally used in english as a way to express continous thoughts, with relevance to a sentence - NOW used a stick to BEAT people with "oh yeah this for SURE was written by AI". Man I used to love hyphens and em dashes (as you can see I still use them) and it hurts :/ 2️⃣ "it's not this, its that" Yeah that's a very normal form of english writing to emphasis the stark difference between the two things being compared. Again, it's being ostracized now. My problem isn't even that I can't use them anymore, it's like you've taken the joy out of writing 🫠 Same goes for any creative work - art, music, videography, etc. People genuinely pouring their hearts out are getting shunned and immediately dethroned saying "this is ai" -x- that's the end of my sad little rant : (

I'm an incoming senior and here's 10 pieces of advice I'd give to my 𝗳𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗵𝗺𝗮𝗻 self: 𝟭. 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘁𝘀 — 𝗯𝘂𝘁 𝗱𝗼𝗻'𝘁 𝘀𝗽𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗳 𝘁𝗼𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻. Join things. Try things. Research things. But you don't need to be in 5 clubs doing 5 different projects. Depth > breadth. 𝟮. 𝗝𝗼𝗶𝗻 𝗰𝗹𝘂𝗯𝘀. Clubs are the best way to build community and meet people with similar career goals. Some of my closest friends came from orgs I joined freshman year. 𝟯. 𝗔𝗽𝗽𝗹𝘆 𝘁𝗼 𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗹𝘆 𝗰𝗮𝗿𝗲𝗲𝗿 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗺𝘀. Freshman-specific programs exist for a reason. If you want my list of 700+ programs, send me a connection request with a note. 𝟰. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗴𝗼𝗮𝗹 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲, 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗸𝗻𝗼𝘄. I did a journalism internship because I thought I wanted to go into journalism. I realized I didn't and pivoted. I wouldn't have known that unless I experienced it. 𝟱. 𝗣𝗹𝗮𝗻 𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗰𝗹𝗮𝘀𝘀𝗲𝘀. Think about a double major or minor. Map out your GEs early so you're not scrambling senior year. 𝟲. 𝗦𝗮𝘆 𝘆𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘀𝗰𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂. That first networking event. That cold DM. That application you feel unqualified for. Do it anyway. 𝟳. 𝗙𝗶𝗻𝗱 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝘂𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗰𝗹𝗮𝘀𝘀𝗺𝗮𝗻 𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗼𝗿. Someone 1-2 years ahead who can show you what's possible and what to avoid. They've been where you are — learn from them. 𝟴. 𝗬𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗚𝗣𝗔 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗹𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝗻 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗸. But don't let it tank either. Balance academics with real-world experience. 𝟵. 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻 𝘁𝗼 𝗮𝘀𝗸 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗵𝗲𝗹𝗽. Professors, career centers, peers — most freshmen suffer in silence when resources are right there. Don't be afraid to reach out. 𝟭𝟬. 𝗘𝗻𝗷𝗼𝘆 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗳𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗵𝗺𝗮𝗻 𝘆𝗲𝗮𝗿. It's the most stress-free year you're going to have. Seriously. Soak it in. Freshman year sets the foundation for everything that comes after. I did everything from: - doing three clubs - applying to mentorship programs - adding a minor that I later decided not to do - landing an internship and a lot more random side quests that led me to figure out what I wanted to do. You don't need to have it all figured out — but you do need to start. We’re beyond excited to officially introduce Intelligence. We raised a $7.9M seed, led by Index Ventures with participation from Conviction , A*, and Y Combinator , to build Design Arena , a universal interface for accessing and evaluating the world’s AI capabilities. We built Design Arena because we noticed that models were bad at making things “look good,” so we built a product that was both for humans to use to access design intelligence and for models to use to understand what designs humans want. The idea is simple: People come to Design Arena with a request. Models compete to fulfill the request, and users determine what works best for them. We use that real-world feedback to evaluate models, improve how work is routed, and help people access the right intelligence. Despite its simplicity, the scale of this idea exceeded our wildest expectations: In 6 months, we scaled from $5M to $60M ARR and 5.5M users across 190+ countries as a team of 10, and there’s no slowing down. We’ve helped the world’s leading frontier labs break the news on their state-of-the-art model capabilities. And the best part about it? We play with the models for a living to find out their limits. What’s the limit? Well, you’ll have to join us to find out :)

"Live in the future, then build what's missing." YC Startup School ( #YCSUS ) was an amazing experience. From listening to Sam Altman's opinions on the modern startup space and Twitter haters, to making friends with Lightberry 's robots, the energy was unmatched. My biggest takeaways from the speaker lineup were the following: 1. Dmitri Dolgov : Scaling as a game of 9's. The demo is the first 1%. 2. Alexandr Wang : where GCP and code are instantaneous, data is not. 3. Garry Tan : AGI is not an event; it is arriving diffused. 4. Jensen Huang : resilience is the single most important thing. 5. Jeff Dean : vertical AI (hardware specifically) can be an opportunity for startups. Towards the end of the event, a lot of the nervousness I had about AI turned into excitement. Thank you to the people I met along the way that made this experience especially meaningful. Until next time Y Combinator .
